newsitem.title: UK: Europe dominates British ruling party's agenda.
newsitem.headline: Europe dominates British ruling party's agenda.

text.p: British foreign secretary Malcolm Rifkind tried to unite the fractious ruling Conservatives over Europe on Wednesday as the party sought to reverse Labour's huge opinion poll lead.
Adopting a less hostile tone to Europe than in recent speeches, Rifkind told the party's annual conference: "We must not be anti-European. We cannot be anti-European."

Backing Prime Minister John Major's policy of keeping open the government's options on whether or not to join a single currency, Rifkind said an eventual decision would have to be taken after "a cool assessment of the British interest".

Resisting calls from "Eurosceptics" opposed to European integration for Major to rule out entry into a single currency now, he said: "British interests on these crucial matters would be seriously damaged if we take premature decisions."
Major is due to tackle Europe later on Wednesday in a question and answer session at the conference, the last before the election which must be held by May next year.

Rifkind's bid to paper over the chronic splits in his party, which was greeted with a standing ovation from conference participants, was part of a concerted attempt to show a united face against attacks from the Labour party.

Labour is soaring in opinion polls after a triumphal annual party conference last week and a new sleaze scandal involving former government minister Ian Hamilton. Latest polls give Labour a lead of between 18 and 33 points.
Under its centrist leader Tony Blair, Labour has adopted a positive line on Europe -- although keeping open its options on a single currency -- designed to highlight Conservative splits.

But Rifkind warned that the Conservatives should not be stampeded by Labour. "To force a decision now just to differentiate ourselves from Labour would be to put party before country and I suggest the country would not be impressed."
Even Eurosceptic Conservatives were at pains to play down the splits on Wednesday in the interests of unity.

"It's time to unite and it's time to emphasise what makes us different and distinctive on Europe from the Labour party... I think the argument is dying down," said former Chancellor of the Exchequer Norman Lamont.

"I think we are reaching a state of greater equilibrium," said Lamont, who has been a bitter critic of Europe since leaving the government after the pound was forced out of the bloc's Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1992.

But commentators said it would be hard for the ruling party to keep the divisions over Europe completely under wraps with leading ministers eyeing the possibility of a leadership battle if the Conservatives are defeated in the general election.
To divert attention from their internal rows, ministers on Wednesday were planning to announce a series of populist measures designed to win back the political initiative.
Social Security Secretary Peter Lilley was to unveil a new crackdown on welfare fraud and Trade Secretary Ian Lang was preparing plans to curb strikes in key public services.
But the key theme at the conference remains unity.

Major told supporters at a Tuesday night dinner he did not want the government's achievements over 17 years in power dissipated under Labour. "For four successive elections the Labour party has been soundly defeated," he said.
"A fifth successive election defeat for them and I feel we will have killed socialism for good. That... is a prize worth uniting for in the next general election."
